title: CI/CD Pipeline Setup: Build a Safer, Faster Delivery Workflow
description: A practical guide to pipeline stages, test gates, secrets, deployment strategies, rollback design, and delivery metrics.
author: PilotStack Team

sections.title: Map the delivery path
sections.body: Document how code moves from a developer's machine to production. Identify the repository, build system, test suites, artifact store, deployment targets, approval steps, and the people who respond when a release fails. Mark manual handoffs and repeated work; these are often better first targets for automation than a complete platform replacement. Record a baseline for lead time, failed deployments, recovery time, and release frequency.

sections.title: Choose stages and release gates
sections.body: A maintainable pipeline commonly checks formatting and static analysis, installs pinned dependencies, runs unit tests, builds an artifact, runs integration tests, scans dependencies, then deploys to a controlled environment. Keep fast, deterministic checks early. Each gate should explain what failed and how to reproduce it. Critical tests should not be silently skipped; any exception needs a visible owner and expiry.

sections.title: Make builds reproducible
sections.body: Pin runtime and dependency versions, commit lockfiles, and use the same build commands locally and in CI. Separate configuration from source code and document environment differences. Cache dependencies for speed, but ensure cache keys include inputs that affect correctness. Prefer creating an immutable artifact once and promoting it through environments instead of rebuilding different artifacts for staging and production.

sections.title: Protect secrets and permissions
sections.body: Store credentials in the CI provider's secret store or a managed secret system; never commit them or print them in logs. Give each workflow only the repository, cloud, and deployment permissions it needs. Treat pull-request code from untrusted contributors carefully when deployment secrets are available. Review who can change protected branches, release workflows, and production approvals.

sections.title: Select deployment and rollback methods
sections.body: A small site may need only a tested deployment and rollback. Higher-risk services may require rolling, canary, or blue-green releases with health checks before traffic shifts. Define success signals such as availability, error rate, latency, and critical user journeys. Keep previous artifacts and configuration available, document database changes that cannot be reversed, and test rollback in a non-production environment.

sections.title: Connect alerts to incident response
sections.body: Route failures to an accountable owner and include the deployment identifier, relevant logs, and a runbook. After an incident, record the failure mode and add a regression test or guardrail rather than relying on a retrospective alone. Make it clear who can pause a release, roll it back, and communicate status to affected users.

sections.title: Measure and improve the pipeline
sections.body: Review lead time, change failure rate, recovery time, flaky-test rate, queue time, and the time engineers spend maintaining CI. Optimize measured bottlenecks rather than assuming every slower check is wasteful. Give flaky tests owners and deadlines, remove obsolete jobs, and review permissions regularly. Start with one workflow, validate it with the team, and expand only patterns that improve reliability.

faqs.question: Should every test run on every commit?
faqs.answer: Run fast, reliable checks on every relevant change. Expensive end-to-end tests can run at defined stages if critical release risks remain covered and the policy is explicit.

faqs.question: How should flaky tests be handled?
faqs.answer: Track flakiness, make failures reproducible, assign owners, and fix root causes. Any temporary quarantine should be visible, time-limited, and paired with alternate coverage for the affected risk.

faqs.question: Should CI rebuild the artifact for production?
faqs.answer: Prefer promoting the same immutable artifact through environments. This reduces differences between what was tested and what is released.
